title: Ballad of Late Love
text:
Love, you come late,

bring me at least peace:

Twilight love, by what lost

road do you reach my solitude?


Love, you who have sought me without my seeking you,

I do not know what is worth more:

the word you are about to say to me

or the one I no longer say...


Love... Do you not feel cold? I am the moon:

I have white death and truth

far away... -Do not give me your fresh roses;

I am grave for roses. Give me the sea...


Love, you come late; you did not see me

yesterday when I sang in the wheatfield...

Love of my silence and my weariness,

do not make me weep today.
editorial_note: This titled variant preserves the same late-love translation while naming the ballad form used by the catalog.

title: The Kiss I Did Not Give You...
text:
1


The kiss I did not give you

has become a star inside me...

Who could turn it back

-and in your mouth...- into a kiss again!


2


Who could, like the river,

be fugitive and eternal:

Set out, arrive, always pass on,

and always be the fresh river...


3


It is late for the rose.

It is early for winter.

My hour is not on the clock...

I was left outside of time!...


4


Late, early, lost yesterday...

unachieved tomorrow, uncertain

today... Measures that cannot

fix, hold fast a kiss!...


5


A kilometer of light,

a gram of thought...

(At night the beating clock

is the heart of time...)


6


I am going to measure love

with a steel tape:

One end on the mountain,

the other... drive it into the wind!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the numbered fragments and the playful impossibility of measuring a withheld kiss.

title: To Lucianela
text:
Letrilla


Tell me, shepherd lads,

what power can there be

in Lesbia's eyes,

that they hurt me so?

Since first I saw them

I do not know rest;

I lost my repose,

I cannot keep still.

Surely they must hold

some hidden fire,

for when they look at me,

I feel myself burn.

Yet this fire gives

no discomfort,

but only...

I cannot explain it.

Tell me, shepherd lads,

what power can there be

in Lesbia's eyes,

that they hurt me so?
editorial_note: The translation regularizes the broken catalog lineation while keeping the letrilla's refrain and pastoral address.

title: To Lucianela
text:
When, to the beat of the ringing mandolin

and the hoarse castanet, Lucianela,

dancing the gallant tarantella,

displays the treasure of her graces;


and, preserving natural decorum,

turns, and her skirt flies modestly,

the ribbon of her slipper is worth more

than rich Peru's mines of gold.


How your breast beats! How gallantly

her waist undulates! What celestial flame

her bright black eyes send forth!


Ah! In her fire I consume and burn,

and aloud my lips proclaim her

goddess of graces, queen of loves.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's ornate praise of Lucianela's dance and fire-bright eyes.

title: A Good Piece of Advice
text:
With a brandy-thick voice, chatter and shout

against every government, whatever it may be.

Call every creditor who asks you for payment

servile, Carlist, bigot, Jesuit.


Imitate the phrase and gesture

of some furious deputy. And if

some riot is being plotted, at once thrust yourself into it,

and urge the mob to burn and kill.


Wear a long mustache, dirty and gray;

a little saber, a torn frock coat,

whether royalist or militiaman.


Understand not a jot of anything reasonable,

hoarsely cheer the sovereign people,

and you will be an eminent patriot.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the satire's mock-instructional voice and its political caricature.
